profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the lead researcher driving the distribution-matching synthetic data project and the infrastructure-oriented research engineer responsible for the shared training/evaluation pipeline. The team is preparing an internal reproducibility package for the paper 'Real-Fake: Effective Training Data Synthesis Through Distribution Matching' ahead of a cross-lab handoff next week. The immediate agenda is to align on what artifacts will be delivered, how the synthetic ImageNet1K releases are labeled, what '1X' and 'ready' mean for the handoff, and how the evaluation bundle should plug into the shared training stack. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the handoff plan: Maya will provide the synthetic data release and summary sheet, and Leo will integrate it into the standard classifier training pipeline and prepare the internal benchmark run.

members.name: Maya Chen
members.expertise: generative modeling for supervised learning, dataset synthesis, empirical evaluation on image classification
members.background: Maya is the paper's primary experimental lead and has spent the last six months refining the distribution-matching synthesis procedure and curating synthetic ImageNet1K shards for ablation and scaling studies.
members.private_state: She wants the handoff to preserve the exact paper-quality setup without reopening experimental choices, and she is worried that infrastructure simplifications will make the synthetic data look weaker than reported.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the '1X release,' they mean one synthetic image per original training example at the dataset level, spread across the full class distribution as packaged in her latest paper artifact.

A dataset is 'ready' once the synthetic shards, label map, and the short README are on shared storage, because the downstream training code is assumed to already know the standard preprocessing and sampling behavior.
The 'paper checkpoint' refers to the final post-camera-ready synthesis export stored under the internal 'final' directory, not the earlier artifact used for the main table freeze.
Using the standard training pipeline means preserving the paper's data-side assumptions such as class-balanced sampling over the synthetic set and the same crop policy encoded in the release notes.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: large-scale training pipelines, dataset packaging, reproducibility tooling, benchmark automation
members.background: Leo maintains the lab's shared image classification stack and usually turns research artifacts into reusable benchmark jobs that other teams can run with minimal manual intervention.
members.private_state: He wants a clean, automatable integration that fits existing benchmark conventions and avoids one-off dataset logic, and he is concerned about ambiguous artifact naming causing a broken handoff right before the cross-lab demo.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says the '1X release,' they mean a packaging ratio suitable for the benchmark interface: one synthetic shard set matching the nominal size of the standard ImageNet training manifest after dedup/filtering in the shared pipeline.
A dataset is 'ready' only when it is mounted in the registry, checksumed, and accompanied by the ingestion manifest needed for automated jobs; raw files on shared storage are not yet handoff-ready.
The 'paper checkpoint' is the artifact used in the internal reproduction table generated before camera-ready, because that is the stable reference usually pinned in benchmark configs.
Using the standard training pipeline means using the default dataloader and augmentation preset unless a change is explicitly codified as a config diff in the benchmark repository.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss handing off the '1X synthetic ImageNet release.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya means the dataset-level synthetic export containing approximately one synthetic example per original ImageNet1K training example, as counted in her synthesis pipeline before benchmark-side filtering.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means the benchmark-ready packaged dataset whose final registered manifest matches the nominal ImageNet training size after the shared pipeline's standard filtering and manifest generation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to calling their own count convention '1X,' and because both conventions are close in spirit and tied to the same benchmark, the phrase feels precise enough that neither thinks to restate the counting basis.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the dataset should be 'ready by Thursday' for the cross-lab handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya thinks 'ready' means the synthetic image shards, class index file, and brief usage notes are uploaded and stable so Leo can begin from there.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo thinks 'ready' means fully integration-ready: registered in the dataset catalog, checksums verified, ingestion manifest present, and runnable by the benchmark launcher without manual fixes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In coordination meetings, 'ready' is often used as a generic progress label, so each person silently maps it to their own stage-gate without noticing the other is using a stricter or looser completion criterion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to align the release against 'the paper checkpoint' and use the same reference in the summary sheet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya is referring to the final synthesis artifact exported after camera-ready cleanup, stored in the 'rf_final_release' folder and used for the polished supplementary reruns.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo is referring to the earlier internal benchmark checkpoint pinned in the reproduction table config, stored under 'paper_baseline_v3' and used for the draft main-table run.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are plausibly describable as 'the paper checkpoint' because each was associated with the paper at a different stage, and the meeting context assumes a shared institutional memory that neither tests explicitly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Leo will train with the 'standard classifier pipeline' once Maya hands off the data.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya assumes Leo will preserve the paper's implicit data-loading behavior, especially class-balanced sampling over synthetic examples and the crop policy noted in her experiment README, because those are part of the intended evaluation recipe.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo assumes he will run the lab's default classifier pipeline exactly as implemented in the benchmark repo, which uses the default shuffled dataloader and augmentation preset unless special behavior is explicitly encoded in config.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe they are avoiding unnecessary debate by saying 'standard pipeline,' but each treats a different standard as the obvious default: Maya's paper-standard recipe versus Leo's infrastructure-standard benchmark recipe.
